extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology of science; scientists and educated general readers interested in scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying criteria for what counts as legitimate scientific method, scientific truth, and the facts of science as presented in a textbook on the philosophy of science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of science
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of science is to ascertain truth in every possible branch of knowledge; there is no sphere of inquiry outside the legitimate field of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not draw a hard distinction between 'scientific' and 'philosophical' methods — treating such a distinction is described as obscurantism. Science's legitimate field includes both physical and mental facts of the universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful classification and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific method is marked by careful and accurate classification of facts and observation of their correlation and sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification of facts is repeatedly emphasised as the basis of science and as a necessary precursor to theory-building (examples: Darwin's systematic inquiry, the early history of Royal Society meetings). Failure to classify facts properly leads to pseudo-scientific or idle theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of laws by creative imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of scientific laws is achieved by the aid of the creative imagination; laws are mental interpretations — formulae that resume wide ranges of phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imagination must be disciplined by prior classification and observation (Darwin worked 'on true Baconian principles' collecting facts before theorising). Theories are creative interpretations but must be tested and conditioned by facts; imaginative invention of systems should be followed by self-criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-criticism and impartial touchstone
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-criticism and the final touchstone of equal validity for all normally constituted minds are central features of the scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientists should subject their ideas to prolonged self-criticism (Darwin delayed writing up his theory for many years; Newton withheld a demonstration until missing links were supplied). The 'final touchstone' implies tests that any normally constituted mind can apply — impartial, public tests rather than private prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification must precede valuable theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Valuable theory normally follows extensive collection and classification of facts; classification precedes the formation of valuable scientific theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (Darwin, Newton) illustrate long periods of fact-collection and classification before theoretical breakthroughs. Pseudo-scientific theories often arise when authors lack acquaintance with existing classifications of facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific claims to social and individual value
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims of science to our support rest on its social and individual benefits: (a) efficient mental training for citizens, (b) illumination of important social problems, (c) increased comfort in practical life, (d) permanent gratification of the aesthetic judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as pragmatic and cultural desiderata for supporting science; they function as part of the argument for why society should value and promote scientific activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific interpretation must not contradict observation/experience
rubrics_metrics.description: A scientific (or aesthetic) interpretation is acceptable only when it contradicts none of the phenomena of life which it is intended to summarise; scientific accounts should not be contradicted by observation and experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The aesthetic judgment finds 'more real beauty' in scientific descriptions that cohere with observation (e.g., chemistry of a distant star). A 'whole of a wrong solution' (a false comprehensive system) should be rejected even if attractive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of science are mental constructs summarising phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of science are products of the human mind — mental resumés or formulae under which we summarise wide ranges of phenomena — rather than literal properties of an external world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This epistemological stance emphasises that laws are interpretive instruments; their legitimacy depends on their consistency with observation and their ability to summarise phenomena usefully. Treat theories as human-made summaries to be improved step by step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of reality (external objects as constructs)
rubrics_metrics.description: An external object is generally a construct: a combination of immediate sense-impressions with stored (past) sense-impressions; the reality of a thing depends upon the possibility of its occurring as a group of immediate sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To call something 'real' requires at least some immediate sense-impressions to start with; much of what we attribute to objects is inference and association based on memory. The proportion of immediate vs stored contributions varies with organ keenness and experience. Example: inferring the Capitol's reality via indirect sense-impressions (reports, goods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense-impressions, memory and consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Consciousness and thought depend on immediate sense-impressions and stored sense-impressions (memories); consciousness largely arises from the stock of stored impressions and how they condition motor outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure of consciousness depends on (i) extent and variety of past sense-impressions and (ii) the brain's capacity to preserve these impressions (complexity/plasticity). One can receive sense-impressions without conscious recognition; thought is kindled by immediate impressions but built from stored impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of thought: thought elements are stored impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements of thought are ultimately permanent impresses of past sense-impressions, and thought itself is started by immediate sense-impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although trains of thought can move far from their initiating impressions, their components are traceable to stored sensory impressions. Mental association and classification transform percepts into concepts; every process of thought probably has a physical aspect in the brain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary vs involuntary action criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions succeeding immediately on sense-impressions (with no intervening stored impressions) are involuntary; actions conditioned by stored sense-impressions (memory, reasoning) are voluntary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: brain as telephone exchange — some sensorimotor connections are direct (instinct/reflex), some are habitual (automatic), and some require conscious processing (consulting stored information). The distinction informs judgments about will, habit, and reflex.
